speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a small and open country, these trends will disproportionately affect us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How we adapt and capitalise on these trends will determine Singapore’s success in this new era.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As front-liners and policy-makers, our Public Service plays a critical role.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our public officers will need to have a keen understanding of our rapidly changing global environment, they will need to have the gumption and courage to question assumptions held by their seniors and predecessors, to be able to make decisions necessary to seize and develop opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, back home, Singaporeans’ expectations of the Public Service are evolving.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans increasingly want to play an active role in shaping our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They seek meaningful engagement and consultation on policies and initiatives that affect their lives, including their lived environment.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, when I recently did a Citizens Reflections session with my residents, I received strong and positive feedback from those who joined the session to discuss the recent Land Transport Bill.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They told me that they found the session refreshing and they gained much deeper perspectives into the workings of our legislative process.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And their interest will extend to the realms of the executive processes, land use planning and many other policy areas of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, the conduct of the session took considerable time and effort by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) and myself, and it also required sustained commitment from the participants to produce a report.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, greater consultation requires not just a willingness to consult, but the dedication and commitment to put in the time and effort.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Where executive discretion is exercised, and in the absence of a judicial review ouster, the public usually is only able to use judicial review to question that, albeit limited to grounds of legality, procedural propriety and rationality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A recent use was in the United Kingdom (UK) in 2019, when the Supreme Court ruled that then Prime Minister Boris Johnson's prorogation of Parliament was unlawful and Parliament resumed the next day.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given this, how does Singapore guide and monitor the use of executive discretion and what are the safeguards in place to ensure that these are done judiciously?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am not saying that there is no place for judicial discretion nor am I calling for judicial micromanagement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Public body should publish periodic reports on how the discretionary powers are exercised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, during a debate on the Online Safety Bill, we proposed that OSC submit annual reports detailing the number and categories of reports received, directions issued and findings of online harms trends.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: As a union representing Public Service, we welcome the efforts to strengthen the pipeline and provide meaningful early exposure to Public Service work.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We want to understand how can awareness, matching and role clarity be better strengthened, so that suitable candidates are able to see GRIT@Gov not just as a traineeship but as a credible entry pathway into long-term Public Service careers?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the placement numbers, it is also important that the quality of experience the trainees have when they are placed at the respective roles within Public Service and it is also important how impactful the roles are so that they not only find purpose but also see clear development pathways within the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, this is also important for mid-career officers who require similar guidance on career refresh and job redesign.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, whether we speak of GRIT@Gov, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled transformation, career progression or workplace fairness, the central question is: can Public Officers see sustainable and meaningful long-term careers in Public Service?

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, I thank Members for their questions on how the Public Service will ensure we continue to meet the needs of Singapore and Singaporeans well.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We agree, indeed, that the international order and our domestic landscape are fundamentally changing, and changing fast.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore must rethink our approaches and seize new opportunities to secure our place in the world.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To keep Singapore exceptional and ready for the future, I believe we must do three things well: understand the world well; understand our people well; and understand technology well.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, understanding the world is vital to sharpen our clarity on how Singapore and Singaporeans can stay relevant in the new world.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Given how small and open Singapore we are and how everything in Singapore is affected by global developments elsewhere, from security to trade, to food and technology access, we need to make sound decisions for Singapore and our officers must understand the new world we operate in.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To help public officers build up their global exposure and connections, we are ramping up overseas postings and exchanges, attachments to international organisations and stints in the private and people sectors.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also ensure Public Service leaders are globally informed and connected.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, nearly four out of every 10 officers on our central leadership development programmes have participated in programmes with structured overseas exposure.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: By understanding the world, our public officers and leaders can better seize emerging opportunities and safeguard Singapore’s long-term interests.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, we will also need to understand our peoples and their expectations well.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The work of the Public Service is not just to deliver transactions but to build trust.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singaporeans want to be heard, to be involved and to co-create solutions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also continue to make our services more accessible, inclusive and responsive.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Citizens who need help in person can visit ServiceSG centres, where they can access 600 services from over 25 agencies under one roof.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To bring these integrated services closer to more residents, we have set up a 10th ServiceSG Centre in Ang Mo Kio this year.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To serve Singaporeans well, we must also invest in our officers.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Sanjeev Tiwari asked how public officers can have a meaningful, sustainable career within our Service.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Last year, I announced the launch of a Career Fitness Movement for public officers to prepare for meaningful careers with increasing longevity.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Building on this momentum, we are introducing supplementary programmes to provide targeted support for officers at different career life stages.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is only possible through the strong support of our partners, such as the Amalgamated Union of Public Employees, which Mr Sanjeev heads.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Sanjeev Tiwari also asked how the Public Service reinforces fair and timely resolution of any workplace concern.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service is committed not only to invest in career fitness of our officers but also recognises the importance of resolving early any workplace concern from our public officers.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have in place a Grievance Handling Procedure and Internal Disclosure Policy.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These strive to ensure early resolution of any concern whilst maintaining confidentiality.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to review them to ensure that they remain relevant and effective, working in partnership with the unions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On Mr Sanjeev’s question on the GRIT@Gov programme, the Government is committed to invest in the skills of trainees.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For trainees with an interest and aptitude to pursue a long-term career in the Public Service, we will also continue to invest in them as part of our Career Fitness Movement.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Understanding technology is an essential capability for every public officer and leader.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Technological advancement, like Generative AI, is not a good-to-have but a must-have for all of us to thrive in the future.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, we are enhancing our capabilities in science, technology and engineering across the Public Service to improve how we deliver services.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, all public officers are required to undergo compulsory digital and AI training, while digital training for senior Public Service leaders has accelerated over the past years.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This goes to every level, from the Permanent Secretary to the last officer.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To ensure Singapore is ready for the future, our Public Service will equip our officers to understand the world, understand our people and understand technology.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Understanding the world will sharpen our clarity on how we can maintain Singapore’s relevance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Understanding our people will shape our purpose and enable us to deliver for, and with, Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And understanding technology will strengthen our capabilities and enable us to harness the latest advancements to be future-ready.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is how we will continue to deliver as One Public Service and keep Singapore exceptional for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Prime Minister assigns responsibilities to Ministers, including for statutory functions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All statutory functions must be exercised in accordance with the law.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Cabinet, in turn, is collectively responsible to Parliament.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chairman, may I have your permission to take clarifications for the Public Service Division's portion now, and I think we have 100 seconds.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Any clarifications for the Minister from the three Members?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Whether the PMO will consider eventually one day publishing more data, so that the public can better understand how the various Ministerial discretions were actually exercised, especially in the example I cited earlier for the OSC, when we actually called for this to be published a bit more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let me assure the House that for every decision made, actually it is carefully recorded and the grounds of the decision made are carefully recorded.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And over time, we will build up the corpus of knowledge, just like case law.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, the Prime Minister has laid out clearly the realities of the world we face.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is more uncertain, more fragmented and more competitive than before.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such a world, innovation is not optional.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is central to Singapore’s long-term economic strength and strategic resilience.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a deliberate investment in deepening our capabilities so that Singapore remains competitive, relevant and able to create real opportunities for our people.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we move into the next phase, I would like to focus on two priorities that will determine whether this investment delivers its full impact.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has built strong research and innovation capabilities over decades – in semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, biomedical sciences and AI.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These were the result of sustained and deliberate choices.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As our ecosystem matures, the emphasis must increasingly shift from building capability to anchoring value.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a small and open economy, we will always participate in global value chains.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Participation in global value chains is not enough.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must anchor higher-value segments here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Traditional research indicators – publications, patents and grants – remain important measures of quality.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We compete on focus, execution and value capture.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It ensures that our accumulated research depth translates into sustained economic strength.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Excellence in research must translate into consequence for our economy.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has built strong institutions, attracted global expertise and expanded our local research base.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As our ecosystem matures, renewal becomes as important as accumulation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Strong systems endure when experience and fresh perspectives reinforce one another.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can continue strengthening renewal by providing meaningful leadership opportunities for emerging innovators, recognising mentorship and leadership development within our institutions, designing mission-based programmes with structured progression pathways.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When younger Singaporeans see that frontier ideas can be pursued and realised here, and that leadership pathways are real, confidence in our innovation ecosystem deepens.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Innovation policy is not about funding levels only.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about incentives, institutions and value capture.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government has taken a bold and necessary step with RIE2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, Dr Choo Pei Ling highlighted the need to anchor and capture value from innovation and sustain renewal within our talent system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: RIE2030 will focus on contributing to our economy and national priorities, and ensuring our research capabilities and talent remain globally competitive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will launch a number of new large-scale, cross-cutting RIE Flagships and RIE Grand Challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These will focus on research and innovation, which can drive outcomes in major economic sectors and key national strategic priorities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The benefits from RIE investments extend beyond the economy to the society at large.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The RIE Grand Challenge on Maximising Healthy and Successful Longevity, for example, aims to generate research insights and interventions that support healthy ageing and enhance our ability to slow the onset and progression of cognitive and physical decline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, our National Precision Medicine Programme aims to develop more targeted treatments based on the genetic make-up of our patients and our population.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: RIE2030 will also address sustainability challenges through targeted investments in areas such as decarbonisation, climate adaptation and sustainable urban development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For climate science and adaptation, we will develop integrated solutions for flood prevention, urban heat management and coastal protection.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will strengthen Singapore's resource resilience through advanced water treatment, next-generation urban farming and circular waste management systems.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Enhanced climate science capabilities will provide more precise weather forecasting and climate projections, strengthening Singapore's competitive advantage in weather-sensitive sectors like aviation and maritime.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to support the building of strong collaborations between our research institutions and private sector partners to conduct industry-relevant research and development, and to commercialise inventions and technologies from publicly funded research.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Through these collaborations, our institutions build up capabilities and know-how while meeting industry needs, enabling our researchers to commercialise their IP with companies, developing innovative products and services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This in turn spurs increased private sector investments in Singapore and the creation of new high-value jobs while further strengthening Singapore's RIE ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also scaling up platforms that bring together our institutes of higher learning (IHLs), public research institutes and industry to accelerate commercialisation of technological advancements in strategic areas including medical diagnostics and additive manufacturing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, we will continue to support the establishment of corporate laboratories between companies and IHLs, to address industry challenges and support their journey to becoming product builders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our research and development (R&D) investments have also created good jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Research Scientists and Engineers accounted for over 70% of such jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will sustain our investments in talent and basic research.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: RIE2030 will seek to attract top and upcoming researchers while nurturing local talent across research, engineering and innovation domains.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Talent schemes such as the National Research Foundation (NRF) Fellowships and Investigatorships, Returning Singapore Scientist Scheme and the NRF Professorship enable awardees to establish strong teams and access advanced facilities needed for ambitious and high-impact research.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: International postgraduate scholarships for Singaporeans will also be enhanced to broaden global exposure and open up new avenues for value creation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These moves will help to strengthen Singapore’s deep tech and commercialisation talent pipeline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to attract top-tier and promising research talent and enhance links between our researchers and the global community, which will anchor a strong base of scientific capabilities here that will spur future breakthroughs and create value in the long term.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Mr Chairman, climate has two faces and Singapore must deal with both of these with one budget.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As in so many things for a small and open economy, Singapore is a price taker of global norms of behaviour.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We cannot ourselves dictate how fast the sea-levels rise, how much human activity to curtail, how little carbon is emitted into the air.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We must instead prepare and protect, as much as we can, this little piece of land, one degree north of the equator.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is the second face of climate change, that although much happens is a result of all countries acting in concert, the impact on specific countries must be dealt with by each country on its own.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: No global saviour is going to come and give us a helping hand.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are very few countries that can say with confidence and indeed, with enough bankability, to say what we are saying with this Budget – that we, as a country and as a people, are prepared to spend hundreds of billions of dollars for generations of the future to protect our sea line, our homes and businesses, because although we are price-takers in the global commons, we are not passive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We have the resolution and resources to ensure climate adaptability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is in many ways the Singapore Story.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As our forebears have done for us, so now, we must do for our future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Here, I would like to thank the National Climate Change Secretariat for its achievements in 2025, especially at the 30th United Nations Climate Change Conference at Belem, Brazil.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This shows Singapore's commitment, even though we contribute only 0.1% of the world's emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Can I ask the Minister, what is the expected impact to Singapore's climate goals from the United States' (US') stance on climate, including most recently its withdrawal from international climate organisations?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: As a small nation, there is so much we can do to harness solar energy through rooftop installations and water-based solutions.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Given our limited land resources, it is understandable that we are focusing on importing green energy from neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: However, this approach carries risk, including high costs and the vulnerability of relying on external sources, especially in adverse situations.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I would appreciate insights from the Ministry on the specific actions taken to reach net zero.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I do support the importance of energy efficiency, and the Energy Efficiency Grant is a positive step in this direction.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial for Singapore to demonstrate its commitment to climate change mitigation and carbon reduction.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we not only showcase our responsible actions to the world, but also protect ourselves from severe flooding and rising sea levels with the counter measures in place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Mr Chairman, the Prime Minister signalled in his Budget speech that the Government is considering the lower end of the planned carbon tax range for 2030, citing weaker global climate momentum.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While we still have time before deciding, how does the Government ensure that there is enough pressure on large emitters to decarbonise?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: With the recent carbon tax increase, how does the Government evaluate its impact and progress on decarbonisation, given that the allowance system makes the decision-making process more complex, both for firms and for price setters?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Have key performance indicators (KPIs) for allowances been met?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: What is the Government's evaluation of the carbon taxes effect on the development of domestic renewables projects and projects importing low carbon electricity to Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Has the constrained supply of high-quality international carbon credits pushed Singapore towards higher reliance on low carbon electricity import projects?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: These are pertinent questions as our electricity use accelerates, particularly with the expansion of data centre capacity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While the Government should support higher levels of low carbon electricity use in data centres beyond the 50% stated in the second data centre call for application, is the increase in demand for electricity hampering our decarbonisation efforts?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Are big tech firms also out competing smaller users, like small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and households, for cheaper renewable electricity?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Even without the AI-driven expansion, green electricity is in high demand due to increased electrification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The Government should consider tougher measures on data centres and other key polluters alongside the carbon tax.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Frameworks already exist in the form of efficiency standards and grants to support progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: What is needed is ambition to scale up incentives and disincentives, alongside more clarity on what our emissions roadmap looks like in the industrial sector.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in a more fragmented global environment, climate policy is no longer moving in lockstep.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The US has pulled back from certain multilateral processes, while Europe and regional partners are progressing at differing speeds.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, as a small and trade-exposed economy, must navigate this divergence carefully.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But in the near term, calibration must remain dynamic.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How does Government continuously assess whether Singapore's carbon pricing remains aligned with major trading partners to minimise carbon leakage and unintended relocation of emissive activities?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the tax trajectory, coordination is equally important.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If decarbonisation is left to firms individually, costs may fragment and SMEs may fall behind.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: One way is to manage through structured supply chain coordination.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Large procurers – our "queen bees" – can lead by setting common reporting standards, sharing tools and co-funding capability building across their supplier networks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will Government consider scaling such supply chain-led models, so that decarbonisation becomes coordinated and investable, rather than uneven and burdensome?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chair, we are in a race to a low-carbon future while I am in a race against time.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This would be buffered by other measures, such as developing other energy sources, importing low-carbon electricity and scaling up the use of electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, one area of growing concern is the significant carbon footprint incurred by the use of generative AI (GenAI).

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is taking much-needed steps forward but also risks leaving a larger environmental footprint with every step.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How can Singapore ensure AI development is climate-aligned?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The carbon footprint of GenAI can vary significantly, depending on factors, such as model size, training frequency, cooling systems and the energy mix powering data centres.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: If yes, how does it fare against our existing footprint?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Ministry intend to quantify Singapore-specific emissions arising from AI development?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a framework to measure and publicly disclose the carbon footprint associated with large-scale AI infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How is the projected energy demand from AI being incorporated into Singapore's long-term carbon modelling and emissions trajectory planning?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What is the expected carbon tax rates, considering all known factors?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The increase in carbon tax rates will translate into higher costs borne by corporations and communities.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What measures will the Government take to alleviate the burden on businesses, households and individuals for a successful race to a low-carbon transition?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But around the world broadly, the momentum for climate action has slowed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, many companies want to transition, yet some may lack the expertise.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others, particularly large emitters, find it not so easy to pivot and require high capital investments to improve efficiencies and transform their operations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In some sectors, commercially viable low carbon substitutes are not yet available at scale.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I seek the Government's views in three areas.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a world where climate action is slowing or increasingly becoming politicised, how will Singapore maintain credibility of our carbon tax policy while ensuring that industries remain competitive and our country is economically viable, especially vis-à-vis other countries in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, I raised a Parliamentary Question regarding the structuring of transition allowances.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry share more about future plans for the use of transitional allowances and purchasing of international carbon credits to ease near-term pressures, while ensuring that the integrity of our carbon price signal remains strong?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond carbon policies, the transition will also depend on whether firms and workers can adapt.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also reviewed more than a hundred existing interventions and programmes which have been implemented by agencies and stakeholders thus far.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How successful have current interventions been, in terms of translating into jobs filled and income growth for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can Singapore grow into a green skills hub for ASEAN and the wider Asian region?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the heart of it, is how Singapore can sustain credible climate action while remaining competitive and building capabilities needed for the transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: No single country, especially one as small and trade-exposed as ours, can solve this alone.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, in this Budget focusing on helping workers to transit in a changing world, I want to talk about how our decarbonisation plans translate into opportunity, not anxiety, especially for workers and companies in carbon-exposed sectors.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The UK established a dedicated North Sea Transition Authority in 2022 to manage industrial and workforce transition in a coordinated manner.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's context is different, but as carbon pricing rises, we may want to consider whether stronger sector-level coordination is needed for marine and energy-intensive industries.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, Sembcorp Industries has pivoted steadily into renewables, expanding its solar and battery energy storage portfolio.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Seatrium is delivering cleaner energy projects and offshore renewable projects right at the Sembawang Shipyard.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This demonstrates that our traditional capabilities can evolve to support the energy transition.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Many technicians in these sectors already have strong skills in electrical systems, safety compliance, fabrication and project management.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In this way, workers need not look for greener pastures elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They can build greener careers here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The green transition can and must be a mobility ladder, and decarbonisation should strengthen, not weaken, Singapore's industrial workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, let me thank Members for their interest in the subject of climate change, which has long-term implications for Singapore's competitiveness, our energy security and our resilience.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Whatever the political debates of the day, the physical reality of climate change will continue its course.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, its effects are becoming more pronounced, more frequent and more costly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Globally, last year was among the hottest on record, with rising ocean temperatures and intensifying extreme weather events driving higher economic losses worldwide.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These impacts are especially acute in Southeast Asia, one of the world's most climate-vulnerable regions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As a highly open economy dependent on regional stability and global supply chains, Singapore is directly exposed to these risks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In short, climate change is no longer a future risk.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is already affecting lives and livelihoods, here and now – and the costs of inaction will only continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we must acknowledge the reality on the ground, especially on the political front.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some countries have slowed down the implementation of climate actions and started to review their climate policies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The recent decision by the US to withdraw from the Paris Agreement has introduced additional uncertainty into global climate cooperation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30), countries could not reach consensus on the phasing out of fossil fuels.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some multinational companies have also scaled back their sustainability commitments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we must be clear that while global progress has been uneven, it would be a mistake to conclude that climate action is no longer relevant.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some developed countries such as the UK and European Union (EU) members continue to make sustained emissions cuts towards their 2030 NDC targets.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over 130 countries have set NDC targets for 2035.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In total, these targets cover around 80% of global emissions, including the US before it withdrew from the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: China, the world's largest emitter, has committed for the first time to absolute emissions reductions beyond its peak.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: South Korea's 2035 NDC target range is aligned to a linear pathway to net zero, with room to improve.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Major economies are also continuing to make sustained investments in clean energy and technology.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Clean energy now attracts around two thirds of global energy investment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In many countries, technologies such as solar and wind are already cheaper than some fossil fuel alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For many countries and companies, investing in clean technologies is increasingly the rational choice – improving energy security, lowering long-term costs and creating growth and good jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Overall, while the current global picture is mixed and political momentum is uneven, economics, technology and nature will eventually drive the global transformation towards a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Against this backdrop, Singapore approaches climate change as a climate realist.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, climate change is real, worsening, and will shape the operating environment for our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While what we do alone cannot solve this global crisis, we must make our contributions as a responsible member of the international community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This spurs others to do likewise and helps us secure our own long-term competitiveness and resilience in a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mature and easily deployable decarbonisation options are simply not available to us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our transition will be more challenging and will require more lead time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, Singapore needs to prepare early for a world that will become increasingly carbon-constrained and climate-impaired.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we delay action, the eventual adjustment will be sharper, more costly and more disruptive for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we must calibrate our climate actions carefully, taking into consideration global developments to manage near-term costs and competitiveness for our households and our industries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, sending the right signal through carbon pricing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As the world decarbonises, businesses and economies that are more emission-intensive will become less attractive to carbon-conscious investors and consumers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Carbon pricing sends a clear economy-wide signal that emissions carry a cost and that cleaner solutions have a value.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying and Ms He Ting Ru asked about the carbon tax and how the carbon tax can encourage sustainable AI usage and adoption of renewable energy respectively.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Carbon tax plays an important role through the right-pricing signal.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Power generation companies pass on their carbon tax burden to end users through higher electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This increase, which is small for households but more significant for energy-intensive companies, leads to two effects.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, this drives end-consumers such as data centre operators to be more energy efficient, which helps to promote more sustainable adoption of AI.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Second, this narrows the difference in costs between cleaner energy alternatives and fossil-fuel based options.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For Singapore, decarbonisation will be more costly than for many other economies because of our resource constraints and lack of alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This means our carbon tax must be right-priced to spur companies to invest in low-carbon technologies and reduce their emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will support our households and businesses through this transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It may be challenging for some companies in emission-intensive and trade-exposed sectors to decarbonise in the near term.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This makes it difficult for them to compete with firms operating in locations with low or no carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are engaging these affected companies to support their transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also support households to manage energy costs through additional U-Save rebates as we have announced.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Ms Poh Li San and Mr Azhar Othman asked about progress towards our climate goals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are making steady progress on various fronts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will provide more details on clean energy during its Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also made good progress in the built environment and land transport.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have greened 66% of our buildings as of last year, up from 61% the year before.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are on track to reach 80% by 2030, reducing emissions while helping businesses to save cost on energy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also progressing well towards our goal of having all vehicles run on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, 85% of newly registered cars were cleaner energy models, up from 82% in 2024.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: EVs were the top-selling new cars registered last year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Together, they form the backbone of our domestic mitigation effort.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because our domestic options are limited, cross-border solutions are essential.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Carbon credits allow us to decarbonise by financing emission reductions in overseas sites where there is greater potential for decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To date, we have signed 10 Implementation Agreements with countries such as Vietnam, Thailand and Peru.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have successfully operationalised four of these agreements so far.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This marks our first operationalised agreement with an ASEAN member.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are creating clear demand signals for carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last September, we announced the award for about two million tonnes of high-integrity, nature-based credits from projects in Ghana, Paraguay and Peru.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A second Request for Proposal for both technology and nature-based carbon credits is currently in progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Looking ahead, we are exploring novel solutions such as biomethane, low-carbon hydrogen solutions and nuclear in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we must continue to study our options and create more options for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The climate transition will create new growth opportunities in areas such as green manufacturing, carbon services and trading, and sustainable finance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will help our enterprises navigate this transition and thrive in this future economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have a suite of support schemes that businesses, particularly SMEs, can tap on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This includes the Enterprise Sustainability Programme and the Enterprise Development Grant.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In addition, we are supporting companies to build capabilities, including in sustainability reporting through schemes such as the Sustainability Reporting Grant.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This helps them remain integrated into the global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Mr Mark Lee noted, green procurement is another important enabler for the transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Green procurement stimulates demand and revenue for companies that can operate more sustainably and offer lower-carbon products.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Since last year, the Government has set aside up to 4% of tender evaluation criteria for environmentally sustainable considerations for large construction, and information and communications technology (ICT) hardware tenders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This provides opportunities for our businesses to build a track record to meet the demands of other buyers and investors who are seeking green goods and services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, large companies with significant purchasing power such as Siemens and Schneider Electric have their own green procurement frameworks globally.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We continue to support greener procurement choices in a manner that takes into account industry readiness and international developments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Most importantly, as Mr Ng Shi Xuan and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin have said, we will support our workers to capture opportunities in this green transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, we are implementing new training programmes in sustainability reporting and in the energy sector, two priority areas identified by the Green Skills Committee.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To pull together the many strands of work, the Singapore Business Federation has recommended establishing a public-private Carbon Transition Council to support companies in transition planning and seize green opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are assessing the proposal and will provide an update in due course.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Climate change cannot be solved by any single country.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even as we press on domestically, we are working with international partners to push ahead with global climate action.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore contributes by catalysing flows of finance and shaping credible frameworks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28), we launched the Financing Asia's Transition Partnership (FAST-P) to bring together public, private and philanthropic partners to finance Asia's green transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will be deployed to support green and sustainable infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also doing our part to support the development of high-integrity carbon markets and rolling out novel types of carbon credits such as energy transition credits to support early coal phase-outs in the region.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These efforts reduce regional climate risks, strengthen economic resilience and reinforce Singapore's role as a trusted and credible partner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even under optimistic scenarios, the world will face increasingly severe climate impacts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are ramping up targeted measures, particularly to address heat stress.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment will elaborate on this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chairman, the road ahead will be bumpy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The cost impact will need to be managed carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the direction towards a low-carbon future is clear and we are heartened that the world has made meaningful progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore's task is not to posture, but to prepare and to act.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will watch developments in global climate action and key technologies that will inform the pace at which we ought to move.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will do what we must, to secure our survival and prosperity in the low-carbon and climate-impaired world of the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: By decarbonising steadily and adapting decisively, we will ensure that Singapore remains competitive, liveable and resilient for many decades ahead.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: The first is really in the acknowledgement that Singapore is a small player and at the same time, we continue to be a trusted partner to others who are on the same journey as us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Could Deputy Prime Minister please share more, whether there are plans, especially if the recent Green Skills Report and opportunities for us to expand to provide talent to wider Asia, beyond just creating good jobs for our people, this will also allow us to build closer relationships regionally for greater effort.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And my second clarification is on transparency and plans for transition allowances, moving forward.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On the carbon allowance, MTI will respond to that issue during MTI's COS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think we are indeed doing this, together with our international partners.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: I just have one clarification for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: I am heartened to learn that Singapore is doubling down on its decarbonisation plans, and I also refer to the Singapore Business Federation Carbon Transition Council, which was mentioned in the Deputy Prime Minister's reply.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: And I wanted to seek clarification because the council sounded like it was looking at just professional skills transition.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: I hope that would not exclude any engineers or technicians who are looking to build their careers in this transition plan as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will discuss with the Singapore Business Federation further and to see how we can structure it, so that it is effective and be inclusive, so that it will be effective in helping our companies and helping our professionals to be trained and to be ready for this transition.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: As far as I made aware that we are planning to import green energy from different countries – being vulnerable to these kinds of power sources, can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify how do we mitigate the risk of importing such power from these countries?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, we rely primarily on natural gas and even our natural gas supplies are imported.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do not produce our own natural gas, so there is a certain need to ensure supply resilience, and this is something that we always think about, we always consider and we need to invest.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To some extent, we build storage system for the natural gas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have long-term contracts and we also have multiple contracts with multiple suppliers and that will ensure our supply chain resilience.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And similarly, as we explore alternative energy sources, we must also keep in mind this is energy security.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Whether it is an import of electricity, whether it is import of other possible energy sources, we will always have to bear in mind this energy security.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The other way is to make sure that you have long-term contracts, you have secured contracts and you have alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Of course, we need to do as much as we can internally and that is why we are maximising our solar deployment and explore other alternatives, including the possibility of a nuclear at some point in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are several drivers for this, all of which are common across developed countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As marriage and first births shift into the 30s, the biological and practical window for having children narrows.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, the costs of raising children have risen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes financial costs, such as housing, childcare and education, as well as opportunity costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The perceived career penalty of motherhood remains real, so many higher-earning women postpone parenthood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, recent years have also been marked by changes in attitudes towards parenthood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As reflected in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report, both young men and women increasingly find meaning in life outside of parenthood and there is a broad movement towards an increased acceptance of not having children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are common threads across developed countries, with France and the Nordic countries having the best TFR in the developed world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although, even in these countries, it is falling – with Sweden and Norway now at 1.43 and 1.44; and France at 1.62.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The one common thread these countries have though, is a heavy socialisation of childcare related costs, all the way from childcare to university, with healthcare costs being state-provided and long periods of parental leave.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was reported in 2021 that France allocates 3.6% of its gross domestic product (GDP) to family policy, which is among the highest in the OECD.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The general pattern is that the greater the role the state plays in the childbearing processes, the more likely it appears people are to have children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And on this topic, I am a socialist.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I look forward to hearing the Government's detailed plans to improving the TFR and playing a role in supporting in the childbearing journey.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, during the Budget debate, I spoke about the need to take decisive action by assuring Singaporeans that the basic costs of child-raising should never be a barrier to having children.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Prime Minister said the Government will not give up.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: His words will resonate with many Singaporeans – perhaps, even my wife.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, earlier this month, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) published Singapore's wealth inequality data for the first time.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Wealth and income inequality are distinct problems and they require distinct solutions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Wealth compounds across a lifetime and passes down across generations.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOF's own data shows that social mobility is moderating among children born to fathers in the bottom 20%, the proportion who remains stuck in that bracket increase across successive cohorts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ladder is still there, but the rungs are getting further apart.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The child development account has one great feature.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The families who need the help most, benefit the least.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I propose that Singapore study the introduction of a Baby Bond.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A universal state endowed account opened automatically at birth, invested in a diversified and low-cost portfolio over 18 years.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If directed to Singapore equities, it gives every Singaporean child a stake in the nation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A meaningful endowment invested early becomes real capital by adulthood.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I propose three design principles: one, a universal starting grant.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same base endowment for every Singaporean child.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, we are all equal at birth.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, public funding only and no private contributions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UK's Child Trust Fund allowed private top ups and it ended up compounding the advantage of families that were already ahead.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, withdrawals restricted to wealth building uses only – education, entrepreneurship, housing or retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One more reason this is timely is that the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) appears set to launch in 2028.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Baby Bond built on the same lifecycle investment logic could roll over directly into the LRIS at maturity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And therefore, Chairman, I ask the PMO to commission a feasibility study on the Baby Bond scheme for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be a useful arrow in a quiver to tackle wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I rise to speak on population sustainability and the Singapore core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If this trend persists, it will pose long-term structural challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, we are ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Longevity is a blessing, but it also means a shrinking ratio of working-age residents supporting rising healthcare and social needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Caregiving demands will increase for seniors, children and students.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will need more preschool teachers, nurses and counsellors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reinforces the need to strengthen our workforce so families have the confidence and support to raise children while caring for their elderly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recent Budgets have introduced enhanced childcare subsidies, housing grants and expanded parental leave.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If not, what constraints are limiting their impact?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond fertility, there is another dimension to our population trends.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many Singaporeans are internationally exposed and increasingly form transnational marriages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Zhenghua where I serve, I have received a growing number of appeals from residents seeking clearer citizenship or permanent residency pathways for their spouses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, more than one in three marriages involves a Singaporean and a non-Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are approximately 270,000 Long-Term Visit Pass holders, many part of Singaporean family units.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Meanwhile, the Permanent Resident (PR) population has remained relatively stable at 520,000 to 540,000.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of these spouses contribute economically and socially.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are raising Singaporean children who will form a part of our future Singapore core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, this is a long-term challenge requiring clarity and consistency.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong was a great hype-man for Minister Indranee so I am really looking forward to her speech.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: In my Budget speech yesterday, I spoke about how our super-aged society status and low TFR presents an existential challenge.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Over the past few years, the Government has made significant efforts, including our Made For Families plan.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Today, I will focus on forming and flourishing families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Many youths share how a lack of time and opportunities to meet people as well as economic and social anxieties are some barriers to romance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Facilitating intentional opportunities to meet new people once youths have left school outside of the grind of work and repeated proximity in shared context, for example, through hobby communities or even volunteering, could ignite a spark.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Could we weave some of this into our design of schemes to gently create opportunities for social interaction?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: For example, a version of the Culture Pass to encourage shared experiences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: By bundling special tickets for two and encourage bringing someone else along.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How can Active SG credits help people find new pickleball doubles partners, try a badminton class together?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And could mentoring programmes for young professionals have mentors who guide their mentees in small groups or industry fellowships, which do the same?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Next, as informal family care remains central, how can we better support couples and families who want to stay near family members?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Not everyone may be so fortunate to have family support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I reiterate my call to form parenting circles within neighbourhoods where parents can opt in to share baby items and figure out this phase of life together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: This can be done in a systematic way, for example, through Short Message Service (SMSes) sent out by the Government at certain milestones – six months or one year.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: This time period is important as social isolation within the early years of parenthood correlates with lower fertility intentions for a second child.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question is: why are Singaporeans deterred from marrying and having children?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last February, I moved a Motion in Parliament calling for continued review and updating of policies to better support families and the marriage and parenthood aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I endorsed a whole-of-society approach to build a Singapore Made For Families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through my engagements, it is clear this is a multi-faceted issue requiring enhanced Government support across life stages.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the outset, couples must want to start a family and feel confident they can raise one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As I said during the Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill debate, prospective parents have unique concerns.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The decision to marry and have children is deeply personal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While no policy can meet every individual need, we must raise the baseline support on several fronts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, a home of their own with sufficient space remains a top concern.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Housing and Development Board (HDB) has ramped up Build-To-Order (BTO) supply to keep public housing accessible and affordable, yet I still receive many appeals from Woodgrove residents for help with BTO or Sale of Balance Flats.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite multiple ballots, some couples never secure an opportunity.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This becomes a major speed bump in their family journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I suggest refining HDB priority schemes to consider applicants' existing living arrangements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those facing ascertainable hardships, such as overcrowded households, family conflicts or past pregnancy loss, could receive an additional ballot chance.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Second, more support is needed for couples facing conception difficulties.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through engagements with residents and Fertility Support Singapore, I have seen financial costs as the top stressor, sometimes forcing couples to abandon their journeys entirely.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this connection, I reiterate several proposals which, in my considered opinion, would establish the "right conditions" and constitute "more support" by the Government for aspiring parents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One, promote early and complimentary health screenings for fertility, potentially collaborating with the Registry of Marriages (ROM) and as part of the Healthier SG movement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Two, increased subsidies for assisted reproductive treatments (ART).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must keep education and family expenses affordable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Offer greater flexibility in using Child Development Account funds for preschool-recommended enrichment lessons and field trips, for example.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would motivate them to stay in or return to the workforce and pursue leadership roles when ready.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In closing, these refinements – better housing access, stronger fertility support and eased family-raising burdens – can help more Singaporeans realise their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us continue building a Singapore truly Made For Families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Deputy Chairman, in the 15th century, Venice was a wealthy global hub, but as its population weakened, it grew cautious, protecting privilege rather than renewing itself.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Venice did not collapse in a single moment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It simply faded as it became smaller than the world around it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, with a TFR of 0.97, Singapore faces a similar precipice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must continue supporting families, but we cannot assume fertility will rebound fast enough to offset structural ageing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To maintain vitality, a calibrated intake of new residents remain a difficult but necessary reality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But society cannot change faster than it can absorb.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask the Minister, what is the Government's planning range for annual population growth over the next decade?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What rate is socially and infrastructurally sustainable before housing, transport and healthcare are strained?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And what are the projected parameters toward 2030, so this House can debate numbers alongside principles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If growth outruns infrastructure, if trains are crowded, flats are expensive and competition for jobs intensifies, it breeds deep seated resentment as Singaporeans feel squeezed at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But if services and jobs expand in lockstep, we replace friction with confidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regarding non-resident manpower, we need a more granular approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Construction manpower is surge capacity that builds our home and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Since their interaction with the local workforce is limited, should we give the sector calibrated leeway to meet build targets while holding firms to higher standards of housing, safety and healthcare?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For S Pass and Employment Pass holders, the anxiety is often about concentration by source, by sector and within specific firms, not absolute numbers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we publish indicators or define soft thresholds to intervene before clustering becomes entrenched?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must tighten levies, where necessary, and enforce fair workplace practises rigorously, including in hiring outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must be able to see that locals are being hired, promoted and developed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Integration must be a deliberate and well-resourced effort to protect our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Venice's lesson is that hesitation without renewal is fatal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A great city that fails to replenish its people fades through miscalibration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must renew deliberately, grow steadily and integrate cohesively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us remain not a monument to past success, but a living city that continues to matter.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Chairman, last month, Deputy Prime Minister Gan telegraphed that, our TFR "base has come down further" in 2025.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But our first collapse in TFR actually happened 25 years ago in 2001.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: From 1985 to 2000, we had on average 47,000 live births per year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: From 2001 to 2020, this plunged to around 40,000.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Just five years ago, we had almost 20,000 more hitting working age than those aged 65 to 69.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Even if we assume a discount for AI-driven productivity growth, we will still need to naturalise quite a lot more compared to current levels.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: That is why, in my view, we are facing a moment of reckoning in our immigration policies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This was pre-ordained 25 years ago, when our TFR first collapsed, and those birth cohorts are hitting working age today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The Government has been stressing the importance of integration to make immigration work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But beyond enhancing integration, I think we also need enhanced equity to make intensified immigration work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, I put forth in good faith the following policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is about enhancing equity between citizens by birth and citizens by choice.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The full-time NS can be shorter than two years for pragmatic reasons, but there should also be Operationally Ready National Service (ORNS) obligations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: At the same time, redouble efforts to manage concentration in certain professions and companies and of certain nationalities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is about enhancing equity in the job market, in professional recognition and in career progression.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Third, in our autonomous universities, yes, keep the share of foreign undergraduates constant because it is important for Singaporean undergraduates to learn how to collaborate and compete with peers from all around the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But at the same time, let us look at reducing the number of locally funded scholarships and tuition grants to these foreign students.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is about enhancing the sense of equity for our young adult Singaporeans as they prepare to start their careers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Let us take a whole-of-Government approach to enhance equity for Singaporeans so that we can make immigration work for Singapore and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Mr Deputy Chairman, our senior youths today – not young seniors, but senior youths, those in their late 20s to 30s, are burdened with adulting responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: They face a different reality, one marked by disruption and exponential change.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: They have just entered the workforce, just got married, just started their parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: While they strive to remain committed at work, caregiving responsibilities are often unpredictable and do not fall neatly into existing leave categories.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: By supporting working caregivers, we enable them to stay employed, productive and present, strengthening both our families and our workforce.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
