text: Mr Chairman, in my Budget speech, I asked this House, across domains, is this person's life improving?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I now turn to the domain where aspiration most often meets its quiet barrier – the workplace.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty weeks of parental leave takes full effect this April.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: LifeSG credits, the Large Families Scheme – the financial architecture is sound.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The United Nations Population Fund's (UNFPA) 2025 report warned that financial incentives alone are largely ineffective when structural barriers remain.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Our estates are built for play and communal living.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Housing, education, healthcare costs, each being addressed, each with metrics, each with accountability.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We have not certified whether a workplace lets a parent be a parent.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The workplace may be the last significant barrier within our direct reach and it has no metrics.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is a gap between what people want and what the system delivers.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: In MSF's latest Family Trends Report, the national figure is 56%.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The rest of the market has not caught up.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Young couples today already know what a family-friendly workplace looks like – flexible hours without eyebrows raised, nursing rooms, supervisors who check in not just on output but on how you are coping.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Government itself has described this in detail across five areas under its Made For Families initiative.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But no young couple choosing between two job offers can tell which company actually delivers and which just says it does.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Government already has the Made For Families brand mark, two tripartite standards, the Work-Life Ambassador Scheme, the Flexible Work Arrangement guidelines and the new Shared Parental Leave scheme.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: At least six instruments, and I have not listed them all.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Good intentions, every one of them, but no single standard that tells an employer or a jobseeker what a family-friendly workplace actually looks like.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I have one ask – pilot a Made For Families workplace certification, a tiered national standard that measures where the workplace truly supports family life.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Companies that achieve higher tiers receive funding support and visible recognition, a mark that they carry into recruitment so that young Singaporeans know, "This is a place where I can build a career and a family".

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: When a workplace gets it right for families, that same culture reaches the parent whose child has a disability, the worker juggling a parent's medical appointment and a child's school schedule, and the senior worker navigating health concerns.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Building and Construction Authority's Green Mark launched in 2005 as a voluntary standard.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Government required public sector buildings to certify first.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: By 2008, it was statutory for the private sector.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Today, over half of our building stock carries the mark.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Making the invisible visible changed how an entire industry competed.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Workplace culture is no less invisible and its consequences for families are no less real.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Australia's Family Friendly Workplaces programme, developed with the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), has certified employers covering over a million employees in under five years and has since expanded to the UK.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Made For Families brand mark already sits in the Strategy Group in the PMO.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Build on that by rewarding certified employees with prominent job listings, enhanced tax deductions and prioritised Government procurement.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in my Budget speech, I proposed a cross-domain well-being framework to tell us whether people's lives are truly improving.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This certification is one practical application measuring the domain where aspiration most often meets its quiet barrier.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: My generation of parents is not asking the Government to raise our children.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We are asking our workplaces to not make us choose between raising them and building a career.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I ask for a tiered certification that tells family something no fund transfer can – you can still be you and your employer will make room.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Chairman, we often speak about population sustainability in terms of birth rates and ageing statistics, but one of the real levers lies in our workplace, in how our workplaces are designed.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Our TFR remains around 0.97, our median age exceeds 42.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Labour force growth will slow structurally over the coming decade.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: If workforce tightens but workplace practices do not evolve, growth narrows and opportunity compresses, especially for younger Singaporeans and consequently, our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Increasingly, young couples' decision to marry and have children is shaped less by direct costs and more by workplace realities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: They ask: will taking parental leave slow my progression?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Will returning after a caregiving break affect my career trajectory?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: In many SME-heavy sectors, where manpower buffers are thin, extended leave creates operational strain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Employers may be supportive in principle, but without structural solutions, implementation becomes difficult.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: At the same time, we must also look at the other end of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Many seniors today are healthier and able to contribute meaningfully, but businesses still face practical frictions around job redesign, fractional employment, training support and rising employment costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: If we are serious about long-term workforce sustainability, flexibility must become structurally supported.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: This suggests a broader question – how is PMO coordinating across the Ministries to drive systemic workplace reform so that both parenthood and extended employment become operationally viable for businesses, especially SMEs?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: If we want Singapore to remain competitive in a structurally tight labour market, workplace design cannot be left to evolve slowly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: How are we measuring and rewarding companies for the progress, not only in take-up of schemes, but in whether workplaces are becoming genuinely family-supportive and age-inclusive in practice?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: FWAs must become workable norms, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Jobs must be redesigned so productivity improves alongside flexibility.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Second, we should deepen Singapore's expertise in job redesign.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As AI and new technologies reshape industries, investing in a stronger pool of certified job redesign specialists and workforce advisors will strengthen both family support and economic resilience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If we align flexibility, job redesign and childcare with real work patterns, families will not have to choose between career and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Recently, South Korea's birth rate rose for a straight second year in 2025.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope we will soon welcome the same good news for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In light of Singapore's demographic challenges, it is more important than ever before that we keep those in our current labour force resilient and supported.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To do so, we must strengthen workplace support for families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Housework and caregiving remains one of the main reasons for persons to remain outside the workforce.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This was cited in the report on Labour Force in Singapore 2025.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The majority of caregivers outside the labour force are mothers taking care of children aged 12 and below.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When you add in the caregivers caring for children above age 12, the number grows by more than one third.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Three in four of such caregivers are in their 40s or younger, and 66.5% held tertiary qualifications, including degrees.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Caregivers have shared that FWAs and practices for more progressive and inclusive workplaces would encourage them to continue working.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: From supporting employees who are undergoing fertility treatment, to understanding the pregnant mother and providing that flexibility to the working parent – workplace support for families would go a long way to ensure Singapore is truly Made For Families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Government has made commendable efforts in recent years to step up support through a multi‑pronged support framework, such as the introduction and enhancements of Government‑Paid Parental Leave and the tripartite guidelines on flexible work arrangement requests.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The private sector has also started leaning forward and the community has seen ground-up efforts.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In 2025, they launched a guidebook as a practical resource to help company leaders understand and implement fertility support in the workplace and create a workplace culture that empathises with employees facing fertility challenges.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their aim for this is also to contribute towards a Singapore where "no employee has to choose between career and family".

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I ask that we do the same for all working parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Guide the employers on what to do, how to be supportive.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The capacity to adopt progressive workplace practices varies across businesses and industries, given differences in industry characteristics, stage of growth, cost considerations and manpower needs.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Larger and better‑resourced organisations, often MNCs, tend to have more established HR functions and larger teams, allowing them to implement family‑friendly measures more comprehensively.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In contrast, SMEs often operate with tighter resources and leaner teams.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These structural realities mean that SMEs may find it more challenging to implement such practices and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is precisely why additional support for SMEs is crucial, so that progressive workplace practices can take root more evenly across the whole economy.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To do this, we should focus on shifting mindsets and reshaping HR practices.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Beyond policy and legislative scaffolding, let us invest in changing how employers think about workplace support for families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is not to say that working parents should be given preferential treatment.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must also balance the needs of other employees at different life stages, including those who may not be planning to start families, those who are single and those who are caregivers to their parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, too, do employers, and we need to meet their business considerations and operational requirements.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Fairness, for employers and employees, must remain a core principle.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I propose that we do this starting with HR practices.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I believe that HR practitioners play a significant role in shaping workplace culture and norms.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are often the ones who translate policy into day-to-day practices and guide supervisors on how these policies should be applied.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The tripartite Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP), which administers our national IHRP Certification framework, has played an important role in shaping HR standards across industries.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We can leverage this framework to further strengthen HR professionals and their management capacity, by placing greater emphasis on the consistent and fair implementation of family-friendly workplace practices.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, how should performance appraisals be conducted fairly for employees returning from maternity leave?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How should managers respond appropriately to urgent childcare leave?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How should supervisors support employees undergoing fertility treatment?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How should HR facilitate conversations and present options to employees navigate challenging family situations?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For the longest time, Chairman, we have left it to private market forces to deal with a national issue.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I ask the Government to take national action at a scale commensurate with the seriousness of the problem.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A national problem needs actions to be taken at a national level.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, several Members have spoken about our falling TFR.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is a pressing issue, not just for Singapore, but for many countries around the world.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially challenging because there are a myriad of reasons why we are seeing this falling birth rate.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: First of all, I support the hon Member Ms Hany Soh's call to promote early fertility screening for couples who are starting their married life together.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Her suggestion was actually to partner with ROM.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If we are serious about creating greater awareness amongst younger couples that they should not take their fertility for granted, we should also make it easier for couples to pay for fertility tests.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is primarily based on the duration of trying to conceive unsuccessfully and whether there are known underlying health conditions that warrant such testing.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that couples may not be trying to conceive in the initial years of marriage and by the time they are ready, it may take them a year or even longer to realise that something may be wrong.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to earlier discovery of any underlying health conditions that could affect fertility, such as ovulation issues, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, low sperm counts or other structural abnormalities, and couples can then receive earlier intervention and treatment.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It seems ironic to me that we are telling young couples we will only subsidise the cost of tests that could lead to the discovery that they have "medical indications" for infertility, if they already fulfil the definition of "medical indications" for fertility testing.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I further echo Ms Hany Soh's call to provide higher subsidies for ART treatments and this should be extended to cover treatment at private centres.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Even so, patients may have to pay upfront cash deposits of up to $5,000 or more, and the coverage varies depending on whether both or one spouse is Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Many couples have to undergo a number of cycles to successfully conceive and some may lack the financial resources to keep trying if they do not succeed right away.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The stress of hoping for success before subsidies run out, can only make things worse.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If subsidies for ART services at public centres are to be increased, it could further overwhelm our public sector healthcare services, which are already stretched thin, and lengthen waiting times for IVF treatment.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Even if we provide a slightly lower subsidy for private care, it will mean giving a range of options for married couples – some may choose to seek treatment at a private centre with some subsidies because it is more affordable to them, whilst others who depend on maximum subsidies can access ART services at our public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We can and must help those who want children but cannot conceive without help.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We should strive to provide equitable access to ART, so that not only the better off can afford to overcome infertility.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Chairman, let me begin with this: there are Singaporeans who do not want children and that is entirely their choice.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But there are also many who, in their ideal life plan, hope to have both a meaningful career and children at some point.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Structural pressures – long working hours, housing pressures, workplace expectations – are real and policy must continue addressing these.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Ten years ago, when I was close to my mid-30s, a professional mentor and his wife gently asked me if I was considering having children.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I smiled and said, "Let me give birth to my journal article, before I give birth to a child." In my case, publishing journal articles was my KPI.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I felt I needed to stabilise my career first, because I was unsure whether I could give both my work and a child the attention they deserved.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: For many Singaporeans, it may not be journal publications – it may be a promotion, financial stability, a home or building up savings.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He shared with me a Chinese saying: 我们说成家立业，不是立业成家.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We settle down first and then establish a career, and not the other way around.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I did not appreciate what he meant then, but over time, I reflected on it differently.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I eventually started my family, but by then I was in my late 30s.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And those who have had children later in life will know, it is simply more physically exhausting.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: On hindsight, this was a classic example of the planning fallacy.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The planning fallacy is our tendency to assume that future plans will work out smoothly, that constraints can be managed later and that we will have more time than we actually do.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In early adulthood, career milestones are highly salient.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our education system quite rightly trains us to pursue academic excellence, secure good jobs and build economic stability.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Family formation, however, is often treated as something that can wait – something we optimise after everything else is in place.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But biology does not operate on career timelines.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Assisted reproductive technologies exist, but they are not guarantees and their success rates declines as age increases.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This creates a mismatch between perceived flexibility and biological reality.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In fact, it is precisely because they are rational and responsible that many delay, wanting to be fully prepared before taking on parenthood.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But when we delay family formation until we feel completely ready and overestimate the flexibility of future timelines, we may unintentionally narrow our own options.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Beyond financial incentives, we should address this behavioural blind spot directly.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Addressing the planning fallacy will not reverse fertility trends overnight.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And in a small nation where our people are our greatest resource, helping Singaporeans future-proof both career and family aspirations is not intrusion, but an effort to support informed life choices for the long term.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, fertility is often discussed as a demographic or economic challenge.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But I would like to offer another perspective.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is also a public health priority as fertility challenges today are increasingly medical, psychological and financial, not merely social.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For many couples, fertility difficulties bring emotional strain, repeated uncertainty and significant financial stress.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our reproductive health pathways must therefore provide not only treatment, but sustained support through the journey.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For many couples, multiple cycles are clinically appropriate rather than elective, although gains diminish over time and must always be guided by medical assessment.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Recently, I spoke with a community leader whose family conceived only after three IVF cycles and one Intrauterine insemination (IUI) cycle.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are now blessed with three children, but only after exhausting much of their savings.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many couples may not be able to continue beyond one or two attempts, even when medically suitable.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This raises an important policy question: can our support framework evolve to provide more flexible and sustained assistance for clinically appropriate treatment journeys?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Not unlimited support, but calibrated assistance – guided by medical evidence, clinical judgement and long-term fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Beyond subsidies, we may also consider how healthcare financing and insurance frameworks can better support assisted reproduction.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, the absence of meaningful risk-sharing mechanisms adds financial uncertainty to couples who are already in an already emotionally vulnerable state.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we are serious about reversing this trend, we must strengthen the entire parenthood journey from preparing for conception to supporting couples through setbacks like miscarriages, to giving families the confidence to have more than one child.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I speak not only from policy discussions, but from lived experience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I personally journeyed through trying to conceive, experiencing loss and navigating childcare while working.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also draw deeply from conversations with Pasir Ris-Changi residents and fellow parents who shared candidly about their hopes and anxieties.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I want to acknowledge that the Government has done very well in supporting parents during the first year after a child is born through additional maternity leave, introducing paternity and shared paternal leave, parental leave and early child support schemes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I will speak on three areas: pre-, post- and a child's first year.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, on fertility support; second, support after miscarriage; and third, childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The first two addresses why some couples struggle to have their first child and the third affects whether they go on to have more.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we want to improve TFR, we must start upstream.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many couples discover fertility challenges only after years of trying when options are limited and emotional strain is high, especially since marriages are now happening later in life.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Currently, subsidised fertility testing is largely limited to medically indicated cases.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Could we adopt a preventive public health approach?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Countries like Denmark invest heavily in fertility education and subsidised treatment as part of a national demographic strategy.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore could take a calibrated approach by subsidising early fertility health screening for both men and women at key life stages and integrating fertility education into public health efforts, like HealthierSG or workplace programmes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Reducing involuntary childlessness and delayed fertility discovery directly helps couples have their first child.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Miscarriage is more common than many realise yet often suffered in silence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have experienced this loss, twice, myself and many people I have spoken to have shared stories of grief, guilt and uncertainty about trying again.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Structured support is critical if we want couples to continue, or for some, start their parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The UK, France and New Zealand offer access to hospital, based bereavement, midwives and mental health support.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Supporting couples through miscarriages is not only compassionate, it increases the likelihood that they feel emotionally ready to try again.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Even when couples have a child, many hesitate to have a second or third.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The concern is not desire, but sustainability of their everyday life.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Children do not fall ill in sync, and families juggle staggered school calendars.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Preschool children are especially vulnerable in their first year, falling sick frequently, adding pressure on working parents.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While Shared Parental Leave has improved, structured support mostly ends after the first year, yet caregiving demands grow as families expand.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In my view, flexible work arrangement is not the right solution.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While they may seem convenient on paper, for parents juggling childcare at home, they often prove impractical.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Countries like Germany and Sweden offer substantial flexible parental leave over several years, recognising the support must extend beyond infancy and adapt to families with multiple children.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Extending the concept of Shared Parental Leave beyond 12 months and a flexible childcare leave bank across multiple years to support multiple children and key school transitions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When parents feel support be beyond their first, they are more likely to have a second or third child.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we build this continuum of care, we send a clear message for those who aspire to parenthood that Singapore stands firmly with them, not only at birth, but throughout the journey.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, supporting parents of young children is key to making Singapore a home for families and addressing our population decline.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Strong postpartum and caregiver's support can make a real difference.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The founder of Safe Place, Ms Jennifer Heng, who works with women in unsupported pregnancies, shared that many consider abortion because they feel they lack the help to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was also deeply saddened by reports of mothers with postpartum depression who took not only their own lives but also those of their newborns, feeling overwhelmed and alone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Trained maternity nurses could provide guidance on newborn care, breastfeeding, physiotherapy and mental health screening.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They could also identify signs of family stress, isolation or financial difficulty and coordinate follow-up support with health and social services.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the PMO's plans to further address the concerns of parents in having more children?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the PMO considered plans to enhance postpartum care for parents as a means to support parenthood and address our TFR?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to consider such comprehensive and coordinated support programmes or expand community-based support programmes of young children?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Supporting parents does not end with the first year.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some parents leave the workforce to care for their children during these formative years.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many intend to return once their children are older, but career gaps often become barriers.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers cite skills obsolescence and for those contemplating parenthood, this risk can influence their decision on whether to have children at all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These parents have already adjusted to a single income and simpler lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They should not be penalised a second time when they seek to return.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In truth, stay-home parents possess highly employable skills – they manage budgets, coordinate complex schedules, resolve conflicts and navigate crises daily.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just as parents care for our next generation, it is our responsibility to care for them – with support at home, guidance in their journey and opportunities to return to work.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we do, we strengthen families, nurture children and secure Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, Minister Indranee Rajah and I will take any clarifications after both our speeches.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Now, I turn to a challenge equally fundamental to Singapore's future – our population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the early years of our Independence, demographics worked in our favour.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While many of our forefathers were new immigrants, most had become citizens.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We had a young and growing citizen population then, which helped grow our economy, build up our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and develop our nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Fast forward 60 years, this is no longer the case today.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Birth rates are falling at an unprecedented pace and our population is ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are not alone in facing these trends.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many developed and even developing countries are grappling with these same issues and I certainly hope we can learn from Korea, as Ms Cassandra Lee mentioned.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, Singapore's small size makes us exceptionally sensitive to demographic shifts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must proactively manage these changes, to continue to thrive as a nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Every one, a precious gift and we celebrate with each and every child born to us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I meet many of them when I join Punggol activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For a short while, I thought we had solved our problem!

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The overall trend is also of grave concern.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Those who are married have fewer or no children.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our birth rate has reached a new low.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is a significant drop from the TFR of 0.97 that many of you quoted for the year before, and much lower than the TFR of 1.24 just a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, our population is ageing faster than ever, with the Baby Boomer generation now in their 60s and beyond, and I am one of them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, one in five citizens was aged 65 and above, compared to one in eight in 2015, just 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Assuming our TFR stays at 0.87 or thereabout, based on a simplistic calculation, just to keep it simple and to illustrate, for every 100 residents today, we will have just 44 children, and we will just have a mere 19 grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Or put it in another way, this room when we fill it up, it is about 100.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the next generation, it will be less than half of us around, around the optics that we had during COVID-19 when we had to have safe distancing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And the next generation is just about the front row, one row.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One of the front rows; 19 of us will be left.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over time, it will be practically impossible to reverse the trend because we will have fewer and fewer women who can bear children.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Prime Minister said we have not given up and he emphasised that we will not give up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Low birth rates and an ageing population will profoundly reshape our nation, our society and our economy in the years ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even with immigration, the growth of our citizen population has slowed over the decade – falling from an average of 0.9% per annum over 2015 to 2020, five years, to 0.8% per annum over 2020 to 2025; 0.9% to 0.8% in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, just to recap – 0.9% in the first five years, 0.8% in the next five years, 0.7% last year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Fewer births today mean fewer young people over the next two to three decades.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: You cannot overnight give birth to young people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, if you have fewer births, it means you have fewer young people for the next two or three decades.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A smaller working-age base will have to support a rapidly growing elderly population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Familial support networks will weaken as family sizes shrink and each family member in the younger generation will have to carry a heavier load.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the macro level, a declining population means less vitality in our city and our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our economic growth and correspondingly, our income growth will slow.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, our healthcare and social spending will have to increase to support our growing population of seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This tremendous strain will be felt at the national level but also at the individual households.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And with fewer citizens, it will become increasingly difficult to meet our national security and national defence needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This raises the deeper question of what Singapore will be 50 or 100 years from now.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our first and top priority is to continue to support Singaporeans in forming families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the years, we have consistently invested in our families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have steadily enhanced support for families in housing, preschool, education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To better support working parents in managing their work and caregiving responsibilities, we also recently introduced the new Shared Parental Leave scheme and doubled the mandatory Government-Paid Paternity Leave from two weeks to four weeks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we will need to do even more.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The decline in fertility is a multi-faceted challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It reflects broader generational shifts in life priorities and mindsets.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Attitudes towards marriage and parenthood are shaped by many factors – workplace norms, employer practices, availability of familial and community support and social attitudes towards having and raising children.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to address these issues holistically and not simply blame it on any particular single factor.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will do more to strengthen support for Singaporeans in their marriage and parenthood journey.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister Indranee Rajah will speak later about the whole-of-nation reset needed to support Singaporeans in starting families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even as we redouble our efforts to support Singaporeans in starting families and having more children, we will still need a carefully managed immigration flow to augment our low birth rates.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A 2021 IPS survey found that over 75% of Singaporeans agreed that immigrants are generally good for Singapore’s economy and 62% agreed that immigrants improve Singapore society by bringing in new ideas and culture.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we know that is not the full picture.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While Singaporeans can accept the need for immigration in the abstract, they also have personal concerns and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Will bringing in immigrants mean fewer job opportunities for us?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Will the Singapore that my children grow up in feel vastly different from the one that I grew up in?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I understand these concerns, and we take these concerns over competition and our social fabric seriously.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue taking steps to address them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This means making sure the development of public infrastructure, like housing, transport and services, keeps pace with the growth of our population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also continue to be selective about who we bring in.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Mr Edward Chia noted, many of the immigrants we take in today either share family ties with Singaporeans or have studied, worked or lived in Singapore for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The majority of our immigrants are also of working age, contributing to our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to explore further ways to ensure that immigrants are committed to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Shawn Loh spoke about how we must place greater emphasis on integration, and we agree.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will step up integration efforts, creating more opportunities for citizens and immigrants to interact, connect and build relationships and trust.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are ongoing efforts to help immigrants integrate and become familiar with local culture.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All new citizens between the ages of 16 and 60 go through the Singapore Citizenship Journey, so that they understand our history, our norms, our values and build stronger ties with the local community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also piloted a new Permanent Resident (PR) Journey programme last year to help new PRs settle in and integrate, and we intend to scale it up shortly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The People’s Association is also working through its network of over 1,500 Integration and Naturalisation Champions to drive integration in local communities and foster good relations between new citizens and their Singaporean neighbours.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our immigrants came from different cultures and traditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It will take time for them to integrate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First-generation immigrants will need to adapt to our norms and customs, but their children are likely to integrate more easily, especially if they grow up in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Take, for example, Bipule Jain, who arrived in Singapore in 2007 with his wife and six-month-old son on a work assignment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: What began as a temporary relocation became permanent, as his Singaporean colleagues welcomed him and introduced him to our local culture.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Bipule actively immersed himself in the local community – trying local food, picking up Singlish, volunteering at his son’s school and in the community, and making new friends along the way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In 2017, he took a significant step by enlisting in the Singapore Armed Forces Volunteer Corps, initially to teach his sons about National Service, but he soon developed a deep passion for defending Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, Bipule’s elder son, that six-month-old baby who arrived in 2007, is following in his father’s footsteps and proudly serving his National Service.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Bipule, his wife and his two sons are PRs, and have applied for citizenship.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Their story shows us what is possible when we open up our doors and hearts to newcomers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over time, many of them become our friends and eventually fellow citizens, working together in one Singapore team to build a brighter, better home for all of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also have to adjust our PR intake, as permanent residence is the pathway to work towards citizenship.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That said, we will adjust the actual number of immigrants we take in year by year, depending on our TFR trends, other demographic factors and the number and suitability of applicants.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also keep in mind our infrastructure and the society’s capacity to take in these immigrants.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With these adjustments, we hope to maintain a stable citizen population and perhaps, with a modest growth.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Like I mentioned earlier, our citizen population growth has slowed down from 0.9% to 0.8%, to 0.7% last year, if you recall what I said just a while ago.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Going forward, the citizen population will likely grow even more slowly, maybe about half a percent; that is what we are thinking about.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But even at half a percent, this is going to be hard because it would depend on the TFR being held up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will review again by 2030, taking into account further changes in our TFR and other demographic trends.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to need a diverse foreign workforce to supplement the local workforce and support our economic and social needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Excluding Construction Work Permit Holders, the foreign workforce grew more slowly, at an average of 2.5% per annum.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But as our citizen population grows more slowly, we will keep a close watch on the growth of the non-resident population, which include foreign workers, to ensure that Singapore citizens remain the majority of our population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we bring in foreign workers, our policies are designed to ensure they complement our Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS) also ensures that firms bring in Employment Pass workers that contribute to our economy while the firms continue to build up their local talent pipeline.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to carefully manage the numbers and concentrations of Employment and S Pass holders and ensure that they complement rather than compete with locals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also carefully manage the number of Work Permit Holders using levy and quota systems.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need skilled foreign workers to help fill critical manpower gaps, to help our companies build up new capabilities and to support the growth of our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This ultimately creates more jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Take for example, aerospace company Singapore Aero Engine Services Private Limited (SAESL).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is Rolls-Royce’s largest global maintenance, repair and operations facility for Trent engines, which currently employs 1,300 local staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: SAESL is working with Singapore Polytechnic to align its training curriculum with industry needs to better prepare our students to take up these jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This expansion will be complemented by a foreign workforce undertaking specialised roles, such as non-destructive testing and plasma treatment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are many other companies like SAESL whose growth has generated new opportunities for Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we understand the job anxieties Singaporeans have, especially in this time of global uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The number of Employment and S Pass holders is small, making up less than a quarter of our foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The issue, therefore, is less about total numbers, but about the issue of job competition and fair treatment at the workplace, as raised by Mr Xie Yao Quan and Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are stepping up our efforts not only to create good jobs for Singaporeans, but to upskill Singaporeans so they can take up these high-value jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we will strengthen measures to ensure fair hiring and employment practices and to ensure fair opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, we passed the Workplace Fairness Act to strengthen protections against workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Lastly, beyond legislative and policy safeguards, we can do more to make the workplace more conducive for all.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) has partnered the business community via the Alliance for Action on the Integration of Foreign Professionals, to develop initiatives to better integrate foreign professionals into the workplace and the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MCCY and the Ministry of Manpower will elaborate further on some of these initiatives at their own COS debates.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Mr Edward Chia and Mr Yip Hon Weng noted, we also need foreign workers to meet our social needs, and they ask if we can have more flexibility.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, migrant domestic workers help look after our young children and our aged parents, giving us peace of mind while we are out at work.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also need migrant construction workers for major infrastructure projects – they help build our flats, hospitals, roads, Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines and critical projects like Changi Airport Terminal 5 and the Tuas Port.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These workers make up almost half of our foreign workforce population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Demand for these groups will fluctuate, depending on economic and construction cycles.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, post-COVID19, we had to catch up on a series of important construction projects, including Build-To-Order flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This strong demand led to a 6% annual growth, or a 36% growth cumulatively, in the number of Construction Work Permit Holders over the last five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These migrant workers are transient and do not compete with Singaporeans for jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But it is important that we plan ahead to support their presence here, including catering for dormitories and housing, transport and recreational spaces.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we can do this well, it will give us more flexibility and capacity to allow for temporary surges in their numbers while minimising the impact felt by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we will press hard to raise productivity in construction.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MND set up an action team earlier this month to work with industry players to improve productivity and help companies save time, save costs and save manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Across the board, we will do what we can to raise productivity to reduce our reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Economic growth is the means to an end, which is to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our overarching goal has been and will always remain to serve the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will keep close track of the population size and composition to ensure that the trends are sustainable, that infrastructure needs are met in a timely and adequate manner and that ultimately, Singaporeans benefit from our population policies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government must and will do its utmost to address this challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will redouble our efforts to support Singaporeans to aspire to marriage and parenthood, and to realise their dream.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This has always been and will continue to be our fundamental policy and priority.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must never let up in supporting Singaporeans to have families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also continue to review our immigration intake and approach, making sure to address the concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to study how we can further strengthen our investment in key areas for Singaporeans – education, housing, healthcare and jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This way, every Singaporean will have the assurances, opportunities and support needed to realise his or her aspiration in our shared vision.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the existential challenge of our low TFR is not something that the Government can tackle on our own.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Earlier someone asked the Prime Minister whether we have a target for TFR.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is extremely difficult to set a target on something that we do not control ourselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We ask Singaporeans to partner us in this effort.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We welcome all debate and fresh ideas on how we can do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our path ahead will not be straightforward, but I am confident in our ability to adapt and thrive.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Together, we will build a vibrant and resilient Singapore for present and future generations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is due in part to the typical post-Dragon Year decrease.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The declining TFR means our citizen population growth has slowed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Trying to raise our TFR has always been a priority but with the latest figures, this has acquired a new urgency.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, it cannot be the work of Government alone.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We need all of society to play their part.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure that our plans are targeted and effective, we must first understand the drivers and factors that are inhibiting marriage and family formation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Declining TFR is not an issue unique to just Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All over the world, more people are choosing to remain single or marry later, and those who marry are choosing to have fewer or no children at all.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As the Prime Minister pointed out earlier today, this issue is not simply economic.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some countries have spent a lot on a whole range of support schemes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These measures can help at the margins, but they have not fundamentally reversed the trend.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Countries like France and the Nordic countries, which have long been held up as exemplars of higher TFR, continue to see declines in their birth rates.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In China, the number of deaths now exceed the number of births.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even in the region, the TFRs of Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam are on the downtrend.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: South Korea, which currently has the world’s lowest TFR, recently saw an increase in marriages and births.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This could be due in part to the large cohort of children born to South Korea’s Baby Boomers who are now entering child-bearing age.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It remains to be seen if their recent more family-friendly policies will have a lasting impact.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, it still gives us hope that fertility trends could shift and sustained efforts across multiple fronts may yield results over time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But what is really striking is if you look at the TFR of cities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a city-state, Singapore's TFR may be more comparable to that of other metropolitan cities rather than other countries.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, the TFR of major cities tend to be much lower than their countries' overall TFR.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2024, France's TFR was 1.62 but Paris's was 1.27.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Japan's TFR was 1.15 but Tokyo's was 0.96.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: China's TFR was around 1.00 but Hong Kong's was 0.84 and Shanghai's was less than 0.8.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Without over-generalising, cities typically have a faster, more intense pace of life and greater competition and stress.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a small city-state, Singapore experiences these effects more acutely.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is reflected in our Marriage and Parenthood surveys, where besides financial cost, other concerns such as the stress of raising children and difficulties in managing work and family demands are the most common reasons cited by married respondents when considering whether to have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But there are other factors at play too.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To unpack this further, I engaged various groups of Singaporeans at different life stages to hear their thoughts on this issue.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And today, I want to share with you what I have learned from them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Millennials and Gen Zs shared that dating and marriage often took a backseat to their many other interests and goals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some wanted to establish themselves in their careers before seeking a life partner.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others were looking for the right marriage partner but had yet to find the right person.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many shared they were looking for deeper and more meaningful connections but sometimes had difficulty meeting others and forging authentic in-person relationships after leaving school and entering the workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, there were those who are married but hesitant to have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They were worried about not being able to live up to the expectations of being a good parent.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some feared that having children meant trading off their careers and other life goals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others were concerned about the financial, emotional and mental demands of parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some women were anxious about how they would cope with the physical and emotional changes that come with pregnancy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then, next there were the married, who want children but have fertility issues.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then we have the parents with young children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Without exception, everyone in this group spoke about the joy their children had brought to their lives.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They did not sugarcoat the challenges and sacrifices of parenthood, but when they weighed these against the love and happiness they experienced, they were glad they had chosen to have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, they also expressed their hope for more support for families and better balance between work and family responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was especially so for those caring for both young children and ageing parents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If we are to change our trajectory, these are the issues we must tackle.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They cannot be addressed by policy measures alone.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What we need is a Marriage and Parenthood Reset, by which I mean a reset across society, on the following.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, how marriage and parenthood are viewed and supported.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, how workplaces can evolve to better align work and family.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And third, how everyone can play their part.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will chair this Workgroup and will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But for now, let me set out the broad four-pronged approach that we will take.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we will build on current efforts to enhance government support for marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we will cultivate positive mindsets about marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we will work with employers to foster workplace cultures and practices that are family friendly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And fourth, we will engage the whole of society in this effort.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the first one, the Government will build on current efforts to enhance support for marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Shawn Loh, Mr Andre Low and Ms Hany Soh raised concerns and gave their suggestions about the costs of raising children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is committed to helping parents with the cost of child-raising.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Four years ago, parents received up to $32,000 per child under the Baby Bonus Scheme and MediSave Grant for Newborns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the education front, every Singaporean child can receive over $200,000 in subsidies from preschool through to secondary school.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will look into enhancing this further and consider the different ideas that Members have suggested.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On housing, as Mr David Hoe raised in his Budget debate speech and as Ms Hany Soh highlighted, we will enable couples who are ready to build a life together to secure and afford their own home.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are increasing the supply of BTO flats, with more Shorter Waiting Time flats so couples and young families can get their flats more quickly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MND has also reviewed how it can better support growing families who may need more space.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will share more at the MND COS.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For preschool and caregiving, MSF has progressively lowered fee caps at Government-supported preschools and expanded preschool places.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Budget 2026, the Prime Minister announced that the income thresholds for preschool and student care subsidies will be revised so more families can benefit.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Government agencies are also undertaking a review of the student care sector to better meet the caregiving needs of families with primary school-aged children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They appreciate being able to spend more time with their newborns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some said that this has encouraged them to consider having another child.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we know that beyond infancy, parents require additional time-off from work to care for their children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many parents and Members in this House like Ms Valerie Lee and Mr David Hoe have asked for more childcare leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying also asked how we can better support the sandwich generation who are caring for their children as well as their ageing parents or other family dependents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will study the childcare leave suggestions carefully, bearing in mind the needs of employers, who are still adjusting to the recent parental leave enhancements.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even without any legislated requirement, many progressive employers have stepped up to introduce caregiving-related leave provisions as part of their strategy to attract and retain talent, such as adopting the Tripartite Standard on Unpaid Leave for Unexpected Care Needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Beyond leave, FWAs are another sustainable way to provide employees with greater flexibility in meeting their diverse caregiving needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also want to better support parents as they re-enter the workforce after taking a career break, as Mr Mark Lee and Ms Elysa Chen highlighted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, these parents can tap on broad-based employment facilitation and skills training as well as career guidance programmes, such as Workforce Singapore's Mid-Career Pathways Programme and Career Conversion Programmes, to gain industry-relevant skills and support their transition into suitable job roles.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is also helping companies redesign jobs through initiatives like the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such support can help lower the barrier of re-entry for caregivers who wish to return to the workforce by helping companies strengthen organisational capability to offer more adaptable workforce models, including various forms of FWAs for employees.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Ministry of Manpower is also reviewing how we can better support job fractionalisation under the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Having more fractionalised jobs will be helpful to parents seeking part-time work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another important area spoken about is fertility health, as highlighted by several Members earlier, including Ms Kuah Boon Theng.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Later marriages and births are becoming more common.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As both male and female fertility declines with age, more couples may face fertility challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, about one in six people globally experience infertility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many do not know where to seek help or are fearful of stigma attached to doing so.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For a start, I encourage employers and HR departments to refer to the Workplace Fertility Support Guide produced by Fertility Support SG, which Ms Cassandra Lee highlighted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On Ms Valerie Lee's suggestion on support through miscarriages, psychosocial support like counselling is available in public healthcare institutions, but we agree that more can be done and will study her suggestions to see how we can better support those who experienced miscarriages.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On Ms Elysa Chen's suggestion to enhance postpartum support for parents, there are ongoing initiatives at the public maternity hospitals and polyclinics to provide perinatal and postpartum support, such as scheduled telephone check-ins and follow-ups post-discharge.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mothers who require breastfeeding and lactation support can tap on services offered in polyclinics, such as the Breastfeeding Triple Support @NUHS polyclinics.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They can also visit Family Nexus sites to find out more about parent-child bonding programmes and parenting support services.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Foo Cexiang also highlighted in his Budget Debate speech the need to better support adoptive parents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, adoptive parents receive benefits like biological parents such as parental leave provisions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nonetheless, we recognise that more can be done to improve and streamline the adoption processes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will work with agencies to look into this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The areas I just shared are part of the Government's broader efforts to better support Singaporeans through their marriage and parenthood journey.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides consultations that the Workgroup will have with members of the public, businesses and the people sector, we will also enhance our Marriage and Parenthood Survey this year to gain deeper insights on how attitudes and perceptions towards marriage and parenthood have evolved.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The feedback and suggestions will inform the Workgroup's recommendations and shape the next bound of marriage and parenthood enhancements.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, we will cultivate positive mindsets towards marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Decisions on whether to get married and start a family are deeply personal.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And as we have found in our engagements, mindsets matter a great deal when making these decisions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When we say we want to change mindsets, it is not about pushing a single "correct" path.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Rather, as Ms Nadia Samdin shared, it is about creating an environment where decisions surrounding marriage and parenthood can be viewed optimistically and positively rather than with fear and anxiety.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There was a marked difference in mindsets between those who were still weighing whether or not to have children, and those who had already decided to have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those who were hesitant looked at parenthood through the lens of what they might lose – being held back in their careers, inability to pursue other life goals and loss of personal freedom.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those with children or intending to have them, on the other hand, saw parenthood in terms of what they had gained – the joy of family and the fulfilment and personal growth that come with being parents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In reality, finding a life partner, getting married and starting a family are major milestones that require time, energy and change.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is understandable and rightfully so, that entering into these commitments should be carefully considered.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, many Singaporean couples have demonstrated that having family and careers can co-exist alongside other life goals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parenthood does take real effort and commitment, and while there will inevitably be compromises along the way, what is gained in terms of family relationships, love and fulfilment is both precious and priceless.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We hope that as many Singaporeans as possible can experience the joys of marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we need a mindset change to encourage couples to consider a more balanced picture when exercising this choice.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In our engagements, another prevailing mindset was the immense pressure couples put on themselves to be the perfect parent.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One young father, a doctor, felt guilty that he could not spend more time with his son because of his work schedule.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He felt he was not being a good father.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another young woman, newly-wed, was hesitant to have a child because she was not sure if she could provide the best possible resources to ensure that her child would succeed in life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Wanting more time to spend with your children or providing them with the right resources stem from good intentions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, in hindsight, many parents reflected that parenthood was not about providing the best for their children or having all the answers right from the start.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Rather, it was about being willing to learn, adapt and grow alongside their children, doing the best that they can within their circumstances and relying on community support where possible, as Ms Nadia Samdin noted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, the Families for Life Parents Telegram groups have enabled thriving online communities of parents within each local town.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Through these local networks, parents can connect and exchange parenting tips, share about local family events and exchange pre-loved items with other parents in the community to help them better navigate parenting challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
