text: Practical resources and programmes to support families on their parenting journey from birth to growing through adolescence are also available on platforms, including Health Promotion Board's Parent Hub, the Parenting For Wellness Toolbox, parenting resources in the Ministry of Education's Parent's Gateway and the Families for Life Parenting website.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will work with various agencies and partners to regularly update and refine the resources on the platforms to ensure they meet parents' evolving needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This pressure to be the perfect parent is perhaps most evident in the child's education.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many parents feel pressure to help their children excel academically, for fear that they may otherwise not succeed in life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They worry about coaching their children for major exams or finding the financial means to send their children to private tuition and enrichment programmes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If they are unable to do so, they feel that they have fallen short as parents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I understand that this pressure largely stems from the fear that there is only a narrow gate to success and if their children do not make it through that gate, they will have poor life outcomes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are real anxieties that we want to help address.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To cater to students' varied abilities and talents and help our children develop more holistically, MOE has been making progressive changes over the years to develop multiple pathways.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE has also made multiple shifts to reduce over-emphasis on academic results.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But these structural reforms will only work if cultural attitudes towards competition and success shift in tandem.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must move away from viewing education in Singapore as a competition for limited prizes and instead see it as an open highway with many lanes and many different prizes suited to each child's unique talents and abilities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such pressure can therefore be detrimental to a child's well-being.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some competition and stress is natural but we should do our best to remove unrealistic expectations or social pressures which add unnecessary stress on parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we will work with employers to foster family-friendly workplace cultures and practices.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As Ms Yeo Wan Ling noted, one of the top stressors for parents is trying to achieve a balance between work and family responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One parent described how frequent work travel made it difficult for her to be there for her children in their formative years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some found it difficult to request for flexible work arrangements, despite the Tripartite Guidelines.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others related having to choose between being present for important meetings or their child's key milestones, and difficulty in leaving work on time to pick their children up from childcare.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Despite the mandatory leave provisions we have introduced and employment protections, we still hear anecdotes of how some employees are subtly discouraged from taking leave or how female employees are nudged to resign once they are pregnant.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We fully recognise that employers have business objectives and financial bottom lines to meet.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, there is much more we can do to build progressive workplace cultures to align business priorities with family-friendly practices.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Having supportive employers and workplaces makes a big difference to parents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But being a family-friendly workplace is not just good for employees; it also makes good business sense.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When people feel supported at work, they are more motivated, more engaged and more likely to stay.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example is Mr Edmund Seah, whose employer allowed him to take his paternity leave in weekly blocks.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Edmund took two weeks during his child's first month to support his wife's confinement and took the remaining two weeks of paternity leave together with his three weeks of Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This flexibility allowed him to be present for his wife and baby when it mattered.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Having benefited from this flexibility, Mr Seah has paid it forward by covering his colleague's workload when she went on maternity leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There was also a Straits Times article last month on Hsinchu City in Taiwan.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It houses Hsinchu Science Park and is often known as the Silicon Valley of Taiwan.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include hybrid work arrangements, onsite baby care, baby bonuses and hampers for employees with newborns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This sends a strong signal that having children is supported and encouraged, and will not be negative for one's career.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are many other ways in which employers can be supportive, such as providing lactation rooms for nursing mothers, instituting systematic covering arrangements when an employee has to take time-off and holding regular dialogues with employees on how the workplace can be improved.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I fully agree with Ms Cassandra Lee on the importance of investing in HR as they shape workplace norms and culture and support the last-mile implementation of family-friendly workplace practices, so that employees feel safe and supported to use these provisions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Institute for Human Resource Professionals' Body of Competencies already includes a key component of holistic well-being which entails HR's ability to drive best practices that support employees to thrive, such as the design of flexible work options and family-related leave.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want a family-friendly workplace culture to become part of the DNA of all local companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It should also be a shared responsibility – from senior management and HR managers to line managers, co-workers and the parent-employees themselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to review ways to foster workplace cultures and societal norms that value and support families, including Dr Haresh Singaraju's suggestion of piloting a tiered workplace certification.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Beyond workplaces, we will encourage neighbourhoods, communities and businesses to be supportive of families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are ground-up efforts to create conducive community spaces for families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Caterpillar Library at the Taman Jurong Community Club established by the Ong family is one such example, where residents donate a book for every book they take.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I encourage more neighbourhoods to create such family-friendly spaces.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Community organisations and businesses also contribute by organising a wide range of activities – from the arts to sports – for families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Families for Life website provides a list of such resources for families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Most of the activities are free or charge nominal fees.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I encourage more partners to come onboard to celebrate families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, the latest TFR figures have not deterred us from our quest to boost marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If anything, it underscores the urgency of the task before us and it has made us even more determined to turn things around.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government will redouble our efforts to address this existential challenge.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, to buck the trend, everyone – parents, employers, businesses and community partners – need to be part of this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We welcome all suggestions and fresh ideas on how we can better support Singaporeans' marriage and parenthood aspirations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Do hon Members have any clarifications arising from the addresses by Deputy Prime Minister Gan and Minister Indranee Rajah?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: In my COS speech, I had suggested that we should try to defer the day in which the number of new citizen immigrants exceeds the number of citizen babies born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: It looks like that day is fast upon us, from what the Deputy Prime Minister Gan mentioned.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: To that end, given the update on the immigration rates, would the Deputy Prime Minister agree that any increase in the number of immigrants should focus more on assimilation, specifically, for example, prioritising families with young children so that the young children, who may not be born in Singapore, grow up in Singapore as citizens and can assimilate better into Singapore to build that next Singapore core?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But also, bearing in mind that many of them by the time they are well established, when they are looking at a place where they can trust to settle down, they may have been here working for some years and they have been here as PRs for some years, so they may no longer be that young.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But hopefully, they have their own children here.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I understand from Minister Indranee's speech that there will be a workgroup that will be formed to engage and to come up with some recommendations on how to boost our marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In this regard, I wish to find out, do we have some specific timelines in mind on when the engagements will take place and eventually, some implementations of the suggestions?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Bearing in mind that actually time is of the essence for us as we understand from the Deputy Prime Minister's speech that we will be doing a review in 2030, which is just a few years away from now.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In the meantime, my suggestion is that we should emphasise and prioritise our resources towards those that, as Minister Indranee has mentioned, are actually keen to embrace marriage and parenthood, but at the same time are constrained by resources.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: So, in regard to the marriage component, I wish to ask whether the Government is keen to consider reviving the Social Development Network to encourage more opportunities for young Singaporeans to network and find future partners.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: And two, in relation to those couples that are keen to be a parent in terms of the suggestions that we have put forward earlier, and those that have been highlighted by Fertility Support Singapore, whether the Ministry of Health is already in a pipeline to roll out some of this support initiatives?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for her clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of timeline, let me put it this way, we will share details of the workgroup shortly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the workgroup will be looking at the four areas that I covered and as the Member can see, those four areas are quite broad.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is not going to be that we have to wait for everything to be ready in order to implement or put in place.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think where we can have some low hanging fruit, which can be ready to implement early, we should do that as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because the Member is right, time is of the essence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is an existential issue; we cannot afford to sit back and wait.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But some things, particularly, if they are more complex policies, or which may need to engage more stakeholders, those might take a little longer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But really, in this term of Government, you can be assured that we will be preoccupied with trying to make sure that we have more Singaporean babies born.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not file a cut under PMO, so I thank you for the indulgence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan was just referring to the higher number of new citizens that the Government is looking to bring on board for at least the next five years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is the Government keen on looking at Employment Pass holders, for example, or individuals or PRs who have been applying many, many years for citizenship, but have not succeeded at the first instance, second instance and third.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We see them all at our Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is that a strategy – specifically to relook at some of these applicants?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But some of them do have reasons why we had not granted them PRs or citizenship.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think we will continue to look at, but I think we take a fresh look this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are quite serious about having to make sure that we are able to bring in more new citizens and new PRs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With new citizens, we need to have more new PRs, because that is a pipeline the citizens will come through.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also want to make sure that we maintain certain balance among our population composition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, those are factors that we have to take into consideration when we evaluate the applications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just on the ethnic compositions, to the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I mean, is there a deviation that the Government is prepared to look at in view of the nature of the problem?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I think it is very important for us to ensure that we maintain the broad balance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am not talking about the decimal digits, but it is important to maintain the balance so that we do not change the overall texture of the society.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Are there any further clarification arising out of the topics?

speaker: The Chairman
text: If none, we will progress on with the cuts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, would you kindly please deliver your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, for my cuts allow me to declare that I am an employee of a financial institution in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, I previously asked about private insurance rejections affecting persons with disabilities, mental health conditions including autism.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government’s reply was that this data is not tracked and that beyond MediShield Life, access to coverage depends on insurers’ own assessments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I recognise that insurance works by assessing risk and insurers must be able to price their policies accordingly.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we move towards a more inclusive society, families also need assurance that access to protection is fair.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a positive step, but guidelines alone do not always change people’s experiences.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Families still report exclusions, higher premiums or rejection when adults with developmental conditions apply for life or critical illness insurance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some are asked for assessments such as IQ or language reports and often, they do not receive clear explanations based on the data.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without better information, it is difficult to know whether these families are being fairly treated.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, will there be an independent and accessible channel for families who believe decisions are unfair?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At present, they are mostly told to appeal directly to the insurer, which often feels insufficient.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, I will start by addressing Mr Louis Chua’s cuts on maintaining cash acceptance and accessibility.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My response will also address a similar Parliamentary Question raised by Mr Abdul Muhaimin for the Sitting on 3 March.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Due to increasing adoption of digital payments, ATM withdrawals have declined by more than 30% from 2015 to 2024.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ATMs with consistently low utilisation have gradually been removed, so banks could prioritise their ATMs for areas with higher utilisation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To meet the needs of consumers, including the elderly and those who are less mobile, MAS also works with banks to ensure sufficient cash withdrawal points in the community.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ATM locations include the vicinity of major town centres, transport hubs and key amenities such as supermarkets.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Banks will consider proximity to residential estates when siting their ATMs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: New ATMs have been installed in areas with growing demand, for instance, at community nodes in new towns.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier, Mr Chua mentioned about the ATM that he has asked for on behalf of his residents.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A small number of merchants, such as some food and beverage outlets that target younger customers, may decide to accept only digital payments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a commercial decision by the business owner.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Most merchants, based on our observations, including supermarkets and heartland businesses, continue to accept cash because there is demand from their customers to pay in cash.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They do not want to lose customers by refusing to accept cash.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, we have to carefully consider the impact on small businesses, as a mandatory requirement may impose additional handling costs for them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Chua also asked about the EQDP.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The EQDP aims to develop the local fund management capabilities and it is designed to broaden investor participation and catalyse third party capital flows into Singapore-listed equities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is one component of a broader suite of measures, including having a pro-enterprise regulatory stance, enhanced investor recourse, a Value Unlock programme and the upcoming Singapore Exchange (SGX)-Nasdaq Global Listing Board.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The current EQDP top-up reinforces the positive momentum and it enables us to support more strategies that invest in Singapore equities including in the small and mid caps.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But, Sir, we should not rely solely on Government measures or EQDP top-ups.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Growing the equities market is a multi-year effort that requires discipline, sensible innovation and also all market participants to play their part.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We think of EQDP as a catalyst to get the momentum of the flywheel going.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And the early market reception has been positive, and we should allow time for these different measures to work.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, this morning, Mr Kenneth Tiong spoke about the need to take calculated risks so that we can make bold moves and do so with greater speed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I share these objectives and that is in line with the approach that we took for the equities market review together with our industry partners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I shall do the same for the growth capital work group.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, how do we react and respond when we take risks and we try something new and some of the initiatives fail and when something goes wrong?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Do we take the approach of learning from the experience and then picking ourselves up and try again?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or do we come down on the people involved like a tonne of bricks and look for somebody to blame?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think how we respond makes a difference to whether we can set up this culture of risk taking in our society.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My experience as a Minister at the Ministry of Transport and MOF previously, and now MND and MAS, is that many of our public officers, including our younger colleagues, are supportive of taking risks and trying new ideas.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are also very open to working with industry partners and with fellow Singaporeans on this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many of the positive policy moves and also the pro-enterprise rules and reviewed changes could not have been done without the ideas and the hard work of our public officers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, I see our public officers as valued partners in our efforts to build a world-class Public Service for Singapore – one which is responsive and open to taking calculated risks while being anchored on integrity, service and excellence.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Miss Ong asked about insurance accessibility for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She has been championing this and advocating for this consistently.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS expects insurers to make objective assessments of insurance applications based on reliable information or data relevant to the risks, in line with MAS' Guidelines on Fair Dealing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have reminded insurers that they should give due care to assessing applications from persons with disabilities and to base their decisions on coverage, pricing or exclusions on objective information and data pertaining to risk.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Insurers should also clearly communicate and explain their decisions to the applicants.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The circumstances of each case has to be looked into to ascertain if the insurer has followed a data and risk-based process to assess the application.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The key is to ensure that the insurer had followed the proper process in conducting its assessment before deciding whether to approve or turn down an application.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In some instances, the insurers could have better communicated the rationale of their underwriting decisions and they have since followed up with the applicants to explain their position.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Insurers need to maintain robust processes for handling customer complaints independently and effectively.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I recognise the point that Miss Ong mentioned earlier, that from the applicant's point of view, this may not be adequate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, should customers remain dissatisfied with the outcome of the review, they can write to MAS and we will investigate.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Foo, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Mr Chair, earlier on when I heard Minister Indranee mention that our education and career options should be like an open highway, I could not help but think of a famous song by Jon Bon Jovi, "It's My Life".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Incidentally, this is a definitive comeback song that revitalised his career in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: I hope similarly, our great reset of attitudes towards parenthood and marriage will also experience a great revitalisation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: There is actually another song by Jon Bon Jovi that he wrote in 2024, which is termed the most emotional song he has ever written.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: It is the song called "Kiss the Bride".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: And the lyrics? "I used to be your Superman, my whole world in your little hand.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Now, he's your world, that's right, I'll step aside.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Now, she's your world, alright, I'll step aside. 'You may kiss the bride'." Mr Chair, I hope as many Singaporeans will be able to experience the joy of parenthood and bringing up their child and be able to join me in this journey of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: I would also like to thank the Head of Civil Service, the Permanent Secretaries, the Deputy Secretaries, and Directors and staff of PMO for their hard work.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: As I mentioned, they have their work cut out for them, but I have every confidence that they would do their best and do us proud.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because the debate on this Head was so efficient, I gave a bit of liberty for you to make that speech.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But that liberty will not be given to the rest of the Members going forward.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I can see that you are a fan of Bon Jovi.
